content: Intersectoral coordination involves establishing platforms that facilitate effective linkages, partnerships, and coordination across various sectors. This ensures that voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) is integrated into national health sector plans and policies, aligning it with the broader national health framework and integrated planning processes. Key considerations for health sector plans and policies include: Incorporating VMMC into the essential package of health services. Including VMMC in the national health strategy and operational plans. Assessing and planning for necessary regulatory changes to reflect task distribution in VMMC services. Key actions for program leadership and coordination include: Strengthening the Ministry of Health’s (MOH) leadership and coordination role for VMMC services. Utilizing existing national platforms to oversee and coordinate VMMC efforts across sectors and government ministries. Managing VMMC services as an integral part of the national essential health service package. Building political and administrative capacity at national and subnational levels (e.g., district-level) for VMMC, focusing on areas such as data use for decision-making, advocacy, negotiation, budgeting, consensus-building, planning, program management, cross-sector coordination, resource mobilization, and accountability. Increasing domestic funding for VMMC and improving financial coordination between donors and the national government. Encouraging visible support for VMMC from regional bodies such as the African Union, East African Community, and Southern African Development Community. Accountability, oversight, and regulation actions include: Assigning and supporting VMMC focal points or coordinators within the MOH at various operational levels (national, district, local). Including VMMC in the mandate of focal persons for adolescent health and other relevant areas within the MOH. Establishing clear roles and responsibilities for leadership and coordination in supporting and supervising VMMC, ensuring synergy and collaboration between VMMC and adolescent health focal points. Ensuring the MOH leads partnership structures for VMMC with mechanisms for coordination, advocacy, implementation, reporting, and quality assurance. Engaging all relevant MOH departments in implementing, coordinating, and overseeing VMMC activities, including HIV, adolescent sexual and reproductive health, essential surgical services, maternal and child health, health promotion/behavior change communication, infection prevention and control, and quality assurance. Enhancing the VMMC technical working group within the MOH to conduct programmatic oversight and performance reviews. Promoting VMMC as part of the broader adolescent health agenda. Intersectoral coordination should include: Integrating VMMC responsibilities into existing platforms that oversee partnerships and coordination for adolescent health and well-being across sectors. Forming partnerships among relevant government ministries and organizations, conducting communication assessments, and developing joint communication strategies that consider a range of communication approaches. Health sector plans and policies should: Include VMMC in national processes for health strategy development and operational planning. Review policies related to VMMC provision for adolescents, task-sharing policies, and consent and assent policies to optimize task assignment and scopes of practice. Sustaining VMMC services requires: Delivering adolescent-friendly VMMC services that meet the expectations and preferences of adolescents, ensuring accessibility, acceptability, equity, appropriateness, and effectiveness. Strategic planning of health services to ensure access, quality, safety, and continuity of VMMC services. Comprehensive assessments of VMMC service delivery to determine availability, accessibility, acceptability, contact with and use of services, and effectiveness. Mapping existing service delivery infrastructure and resources for VMMC in community-based and health-facility settings, identifying gaps in harder-to-reach areas. Conducting demand creation activities tailored to specific contexts and intended audiences, informed by research and situational analyses, to address barriers to VMMC uptake. Reorienting service delivery models involves: Integrating VMMC services into routine primary care as part of an integrated or linked package of services, including routine adolescent health services and essential minor surgical services. Utilizing varied service delivery platforms to reach adolescents with adolescent-friendly care, such as in-school and out-of-school settings, community-based platforms, digital communication, and faith-based platforms. Establishing clear referral systems from VMMC to other adolescent services, such as mental health, sexual and reproductive health, non-communicable diseases, and vaccinations. Leveraging digital technology to support continuity of information and patient tracking. Empowering and engaging people is critical for sustainability: Empowering individuals, families, and communities to make effective decisions about their health through a human rights-based approach. Reaching underserved and marginalized groups, including adolescents, through sustained service delivery that leaves no one behind. Addressing barriers faced by underserved and disadvantaged populations, including key populations. Advocating for policy reviews to remove structural barriers, such as age of consent laws, that may limit access to services. Facilitating an age-appropriate, meaningful, and comprehensible informed consent process for all clients. Ensuring safety and quality requires: Implementing national quality standards and systems aligned with WHO and UNAIDS global standards for quality health care services for adolescents. Standardizing surgical protocols focused on patient safety and strengthening surgical systems. Establishing effective multi-level surveillance systems for monitoring adverse events, ensuring both healthcare workers’ and patients’ safety. Critical enablers for sustainable VMMC services include: Adolescent leadership, co-produced health services, local ownership, and participation. Engaging adolescents and youth as leaders and key stakeholders in VMMC at national, district, and community levels. Community engagement through partnerships with community gatekeepers, traditional male circumcisers, and faith-based healthcare workers. Multisectoral partnerships with clear mandates and functional platforms for strategic and operational engagement with other sectors, such as education, family and social affairs, agriculture, and nutrition. Enabling laws and policies that uphold adolescents’ rights to health choices and well-being, considering their varying levels of maturity and understanding. Research needs for sustainability include: Conducting implementation research to inform the transition to sustainable VMMC services over time.
